title: Standards-aligned lesson plan
desc: A rigorous, differentiated single-lesson plan with gradual release.

fields.ph: e.g. 28 students, mixed readiness, 3 ELLs, 2 IEPs (reading)

tpl:
You are an expert instructional coach and curriculum designer with deep classroom experience in {{subject}}. Design a rigorous, engaging {{duration}} lesson.

CONTEXT
• Grade/level: {{grade}}
• Topic: {{topic}}
• Standard(s): {{standard}}
• Class profile: {{profile}}

REQUIREMENTS
1. Write 1–2 measurable objectives using observable Bloom's verbs, plus student-friendly "I can…" success criteria.
2. Open with a ~5-minute hook that connects to students' real lives or a provocative question.
3. Structure with gradual release — I do (model) → We do (guided) → You do (independent) — with a timing for each part that sums to the total.
4. Embed at least 2 formative checks for understanding, and state your move if students don't get it.
5. Differentiate: one concrete scaffold for students who struggle and one extension for those ready for more.
6. Close with a 3-minute exit ticket that directly measures the objective.
7. List materials and prep.

OUTPUT
A skimmable plan with clear headings and a timing column; concise teacher-facing language. First, state any assumptions in one line. Ask up to 3 clarifying questions ONLY if a critical detail is missing; otherwise proceed.

title: Unit plan / learning progression
desc: A sequenced multi-lesson unit with essential questions and assessments.
tpl:
You are an expert curriculum designer using Understanding by Design (backward design). Build a {{lessons}}-lesson unit for {{grade}} {{subject}} on "{{unit}}".

Anchor it to these standards/goals: {{standards}}

Produce, in order:
1. One overarching Essential Question and 2–3 Enduring Understandings.
2. A summative performance assessment that would demonstrate mastery, with a 3-bullet success description.
3. A lesson-by-lesson progression as a TABLE: # | lesson focus | objective (measurable) | key activity | formative checkpoint.
4. A short list of the most common student misconceptions for this unit and where in the sequence to address each.
5. Vocabulary to pre-teach.

Sequence lessons so skills build logically. State assumptions in one line first.

title: Differentiate one activity into tiers
desc: Same objective, three readiness tiers, plus ELL and IEP supports.

fields.ph: Describe the task and its learning objective

title: Scaffold a complex task
desc: Break a hard task into supported steps with a fade-out plan.

fields.ph: e.g. Write a DBQ essay using 4 sources

tpl:
You are a literacy and cognitive-load expert. Scaffold this complex task for {{grade}} {{subject}} so every student can access it.

Task: {{task}}
Common sticking point: {{stuck}}

Provide:
1. A step-by-step breakdown (numbered), each step small and checkable.
2. Sentence starters / frames for the hardest step.
3. One fully worked example ("model") showing what good looks like.
4. A 3-stage fade plan (heavy support → partial → independent) so students eventually do it unaided.
5. A quick way to check mastery at the end.

Be concrete and classroom-ready.

title: Analytic rubric generator
desc: Observable, student-friendly descriptors plus a checklist version.
tpl:
You are an assessment specialist. Create an analytic rubric for this {{grade}} assignment.

Assignment: {{assignment}}
Criteria: {{criteria}} (if blank, propose 4–5 strong criteria for this task)
Levels: {{levels}}

Rules:
• For each criterion, write descriptors that differentiate levels by QUALITY (specific and observable), not by amount ("2 examples vs 3").
• Use student-friendly language a learner could self-assess against.
• Add a one-line "look-for" note per criterion for fast grading.

Output the rubric as a table, then a student-facing "Did I…?" checklist version of the same criteria.

title: Quiz + answer key with misconception distractors
desc: Items at a chosen rigor level; wrong answers target real misconceptions.
tpl:
You are a psychometrics-aware test designer. Write {{num}} {{types}} items on "{{topic}}" for {{grade}} {{subject}} at the {{rigor}} level.

Requirements:
• Each item assesses a clear skill — label which skill/standard.
• For multiple-choice items, write distractors where EACH one corresponds to a specific, common student misconception (not random wrong answers).
• Vary surface features so pattern-matching won't work.

Then provide an ANSWER KEY that gives, for every item: the correct answer, a one-line rationale, and — for each distractor — the misconception it reveals. End with a short note on what a wrong pattern across items would tell me about student thinking.

title: Targeted exit ticket
desc: A 3-item formative check with next-day moves.

fields.ph: e.g. Identify theme in a short text

tpl:
You are a formative-assessment expert. Design a 3-item exit ticket for {{grade}} that measures this objective: {{objective}}.

• At least one item must be designed to reveal this misconception: {{misconception}}.
• Keep it doable in 3–4 minutes.

Provide the exit ticket, a quick scoring guide (what mastery vs partial vs not-yet looks like), and a specific "next-day move" for each of those three result buckets.

title: Report card comments
desc: Specific, warm, jargon-free comments with a next step.
tpl:
You are an experienced teacher writing end-of-term report card comments. Write TWO comment options for {{name}} in {{grade}} {{subject}}.

Each comment must: name the specific strength "{{strength}}"; frame the growth area "{{growth}}" constructively; and give ONE concrete next step families can support at home. Tone: {{tone}}. 60–90 words. No jargon or labels. Use the student's name naturally and gender-neutral phrasing unless I say otherwise.

title: Parent email — raising a concern
desc: Empathetic, factual, solution-focused — under 200 words.

fields.ph: e.g. Missing 4 of last 6 homework assignments; quiet in class discussions
e.g. partner on a homework routine

title: Parent email — good news
desc: A specific, warm note home to celebrate a win.

fields.ph: e.g. Led her group respectfully and improved her quiz score by 20%

tpl:
You are a warm, specific teacher sending good news home about {{name}}. Write a short email celebrating: {{what}}.

Include one concrete detail that shows you really noticed, connect it to a positive quality (effort, kindness, growth), and suggest one simple way the family can reinforce it. Under 130 words, genuine (not gushy). Add a friendly subject line.

title: Actionable student feedback (glow & grow)
desc: Feedback tied strictly to your success criteria, with a model.

fields.ph: List the criteria the work should meet
Paste the student's response or summarize it

title: Lesson hooks / anticipatory sets
desc: Three 5-minute openers that spark curiosity, with teacher scripts.
tpl:
You are a master of student engagement. Design THREE distinct 5-minute hooks to open a {{grade}} lesson on "{{topic}}"{{real}}.

Make them different in kind — e.g. a provocative question, a surprising fact/phenomenon or data point, and a quick hands-on or thought experiment. For EACH hook give: the exact opening line the teacher says, the 1–2 minute mini-activity, and the transition sentence that connects it to today's objective. Keep them low-prep.

title: Discussion questions (Bloom's ladder)
desc: Eight questions ascending Bloom's, with follow-ups and frames.

fields.ph: e.g. The water cycle / a poem title

fields.l: Paste text or key content — optional
fields.ph: Optional: paste the passage or notes to ground the questions

tpl:
You are a discussion-facilitation expert. Create a ladder of 8 discussion questions for {{grade}} on "{{topic}}".{{content}}

Order them ascending Bloom's Taxonomy and LABEL each (Remember → Understand → Apply → Analyze → Evaluate → Create). Then add: 2 "press for reasoning" follow-up prompts I can use on any answer, and 2 sentence frames that help reluctant students participate. Keep questions open-ended (no yes/no).

title: Reteach a misconception
desc: Diagnose the root cause and reteach with a new representation.
tpl:
You are a diagnostic teaching expert. Students in {{grade}} {{subject}} are struggling with "{{concept}}". The observed error: {{misconception}}.

1. Diagnose the likely ROOT CAUSE of this misconception (why it makes sense to the student).
2. Design a 15-minute reteach that uses a DIFFERENT representation than the usual one (visual/manipulative/analogy) — name it.
3. Give one concrete analogy students will remember.
4. Provide 2 worked examples that explicitly CONTRAST the wrong approach with the correct one, side by side.
5. Add 3 checks for understanding of increasing difficulty and a single reassessment item.

Be specific and ready to teach.

title: Adapt a text to a reading level
desc: Rewrite for a target level while preserving key vocabulary.
tpl:
You are a reading specialist. Rewrite the text below for a {{target}} reading level WITHOUT losing essential content or accuracy.

Keep these key terms: {{preserve}} — and define each one in-line, in kid-friendly words, the first time it appears. Use shorter sentences and active voice; keep the logical flow.

TEXT:
{{text}}

After the rewrite, add: (1) a short glossary of the key terms in simple language, and (2) one sentence noting anything important you had to simplify so I can decide if it's acceptable.

title: Emergency substitute plans
desc: No-prep, bell-to-bell plans any sub can run.
tpl:
You are a veteran teacher writing emergency substitute plans a sub with NO content knowledge can run smoothly for {{days}} day(s) in {{grade}} {{subject}} (focus: {{focus}}).

For each day provide: a bell-to-bell schedule with timings, exact scripts/directions, a meaningful but self-contained activity (no prep, no login required) plus a low-tech backup if tech fails, an answer key, and a short "classroom notes" section (routines, who to ask, behavior tips). Keep students learning, not just busy.

title: Write measurable learning objectives
desc: Observable, standards-aligned objectives + success criteria.
tpl:
You are an instructional design expert. Write 3 measurable learning objectives for {{grade}} {{subject}} on "{{topic}}"{{standard}}, each at a different Bloom's level, using observable verbs (avoid "understand/know").

For each: give the objective, an ABCD breakdown (Audience, Behavior, Condition, Degree), and one student-friendly "I can…" success criterion. Then flag one common pitfall teachers make writing objectives for this topic.

title: Pacing guide / scope & sequence
desc: Week-by-week coverage with review buffers and checkpoints.

fields.ph: Paste the standards or unit topics

tpl:
You are a curriculum coordinator. Build a {{weeks}}-week pacing guide for {{grade}} {{subject}} covering: {{standards}}.

Output a TABLE: week | focus/standard | key concepts | assessment checkpoint. Balance coverage with depth, spiral prior skills, and build in review/buffer weeks and unit assessments. End with 2 sentences on where teachers usually fall behind and how to protect pacing.

title: Station / centers rotation
desc: Independent, teacher-led, collaborative and tech stations.
tpl:
You are a differentiation expert. Design {{num}} learning stations ({{minutes}} min each) for {{grade}} {{subject}} on "{{topic}}", including one teacher-led, one collaborative, one independent, and (if applicable) one tech station.

For each station: objective, student directions, materials, and a self-check or accountability output. Then give rotation logistics, a signal for transitions, and a single accountability sheet students carry between stations.

title: Project-based learning unit
desc: Authentic driving question, real product, milestones, rubric.
tpl:
You are a PBL designer (Gold Standard PBL). Design a {{weeks}} project for {{grade}} {{subject}} on "{{topic}}".

Include: an authentic Driving Question, a real-world product and audience, the standards addressed, a milestone timeline with formative checkpoints, student voice-and-choice options, scaffolds for the trickiest step, and an analytic rubric aligned to the standards. Keep it rigorous and doable.

title: ELL language supports for a lesson
desc: WIDA-aligned frames, tiered vocab and language objectives.

title: IEP accommodations for a task
desc: Accommodations vs modifications, matched to the need.

title: Enrichment for advanced learners
desc: Depth and complexity extensions, not just more work.
tpl:
You are a gifted-education specialist. Design enrichment for students who have already mastered "{{topic}}" in {{grade}} {{subject}}.

Use depth and complexity (not more problems): give one open-ended challenge, one real-world application, one cross-disciplinary connection, and a higher-Bloom product (create/evaluate). Avoid busywork; each option should deepen thinking. Include a simple success rubric.

title: Choice board (learning menu)
desc: Same objective, varied paths and Bloom's levels.
tpl:
You are a differentiation expert. Create a {{cells}} choice board for {{grade}} {{subject}} on "{{topic}}".

Every task must assess the SAME objective but vary by modality (write/build/draw/speak/analyze) and Bloom's level. Present as a grid with a one-line task in each cell, mark the rigor level, and add a shared success checklist so any choice can be graded fairly.

title: Sentence frames / stems
desc: Tiered academic-language frames for a purpose.

fields.ph: e.g. argue a claim, compare, explain cause/effect

tpl:
You are an academic-language expert. Generate sentence frames for {{grade}} {{subject}} students to {{purpose}}.

Give three tiers (beginning → advanced), 3–4 frames each, plus a short bank of academic transition words/vocabulary for this purpose. Frames should push precise, evidence-based language, not fill-in-the-blank guessing.

title: Tiered questions for one topic
desc: Same concept, three readiness levels, labeled.
tpl: You are a differentiation expert. For "{{topic}}" in {{grade}} {{subject}}, write questions at three readiness tiers (approaching, on-level, advanced) that all target the SAME core concept — not easier vs harder topics. Label each tier, keep them open-ended, and add one line explaining how each still gets at the concept.

title: Test blueprint / table of specifications
desc: Map items to standards and DOK with weightings.
tpl:
You are an assessment designer. Build a test blueprint (table of specifications) for a {{num}}-item {{grade}} {{subject}} test covering: {{topics}}.

Output a TABLE mapping each standard/topic to the number of items and their Depth of Knowledge levels, with a % weighting per topic. Ensure balanced coverage and a spread across DOK 1–3. Flag any topic that's over- or under-weighted.

title: Performance assessment task (GRASPS)
desc: Authentic task with an aligned rubric.
tpl:
You are an assessment designer using GRASPS. Create an authentic performance task for {{grade}} {{subject}} assessing "{{standard}}".

Define Goal, Role, Audience, Situation, Product, and Standards/criteria. Make it real-world and worth doing, then provide an analytic rubric (3–4 criteria, clear level descriptors). Note one way to keep it academically honest.

title: Student self-assessment
desc: Criteria-aligned reflection and goal-setting.

fields.ph: List the criteria students should reflect against

tpl:
You are a formative-assessment expert. Create a student self-assessment for {{grade}} aligned to these criteria: {{criteria}}.

Use student-friendly "I can…" statements with a simple rating scale, 2 evidence prompts ("Where did you show this?"), a reflection question, and a goal-setting box with a sentence frame. Keep it honest and growth-oriented, not just a checklist.

title: Peer feedback protocol
desc: Structured, kind, specific peer review.
tpl:
You are a literacy coach. Design a structured peer-feedback protocol for {{grade}} students reviewing: {{assignment}}.

Use a named routine (e.g., TAG or glow/grow/question), provide sentence frames for each part, guardrails that keep feedback kind and specific (no "it's good"), a time structure, and a reflection step for the author. Include a 2-line teacher script to launch it.

title: Error analysis worksheet
desc: Find, fix and explain common mistakes.
tpl:
You are a diagnostic teacher. Create an error-analysis worksheet for {{grade}} {{subject}} on "{{skill}}": 5 already-worked problems, each containing a realistic, common mistake. Students must find the error, fix it, and explain the misconception in words.

Provide an answer key that names the misconception in each and a one-line teaching note. This builds metacognition, not just correct answers.

title: Standards-based proficiency scale
desc: Observable descriptors for a grading scale.
tpl:
You are a standards-based grading expert. Write a proficiency scale for this {{grade}} standard using a {{scale}} scale: {{standard}}.

For each level, write an observable, student-friendly descriptor that differentiates by the QUALITY of understanding (what the student can do), not effort or amount. Include one example of student work/behavior per level. Keep the "meets/proficient" level tied exactly to the standard.

title: Depth of Knowledge question set
desc: Questions across all four DOK levels.
tpl: You are an assessment expert. For "{{topic}}" in {{grade}} {{subject}}, write 2 questions at EACH Depth of Knowledge level (DOK 1 recall, 2 skill/concept, 3 strategic reasoning, 4 extended thinking), clearly labeled. For each, add one line on what a good answer reveals about student thinking.

title: Report-comment bank
desc: Reusable comments by proficiency, with blanks to personalize.
tpl:
You are an experienced teacher. Generate a bank of 16 report-card/comment options for {{grade}} {{subject}} focused on "{{focus}}", grouped by proficiency (Exceeding / Meeting / Approaching / Beginning), 4 each.

Each comment: names a specific behavior, stays growth-oriented and jargon-free, ~25–40 words, with [name] and [detail] blanks to personalize. Avoid repetitive phrasing across comments.

title: Narrative progress report
desc: Warm, parent-friendly summary from your notes.
tpl:
You are a caring teacher writing a narrative progress report for {{name}} ({{grade}}) from these notes: {{notes}}.

Write 1–2 warm, specific paragraphs covering academic progress, a genuine strength, one growth area framed constructively, and a concrete next step families can support. Parent-friendly, no jargon, use the student's name naturally and neutral pronouns unless told otherwise.

title: Parent-teacher conference talking points
desc: Strengths-first, data-informed, collaborative.
tpl:
You are a teacher preparing for a parent-teacher conference about {{name}}. From these notes: {{notes}}

Give a 10-minute talking-point outline: open with a genuine strength, share one growth area with specific evidence/data (no labels), suggest one concrete home strategy, and end with 2 open questions to invite the family's perspective. Keep it warm and collaborative, and include one line to open and one to close the meeting.

title: Process praise / growth-mindset feedback
desc: Turn generic praise into specific process feedback.

fields.ph: e.g. student kept trying a hard problem

tpl: You are a growth-mindset coach. For this {{grade}} situation — {{situation}} — write 5 pieces of specific PROCESS praise (naming effort, strategy, persistence, or improvement), not ability/person praise ("you're so smart"). For each, add the reason it supports a growth mindset. Keep it authentic, not over-the-top.

title: Class newsletter
desc: Warm, skimmable weekly family update.

title: Back-to-school welcome letter
desc: Set the tone with families on day one.
tpl:
You are {{teacher}}, writing a warm back-to-school welcome letter to {{grade}} {{subject}} families.

Cover: a genuine welcome, what students will explore this year, your class values/approach, how and when to reach you, key supplies or routines, and an invitation to share anything about their child. Positive, concise, jargon-free. Include a friendly subject line.

title: Difficult conversation script
desc: NVC-structured script with de-escalation lines.

fields.ph: What needs to be discussed and the outcome you want

tpl:
You are a communication coach. Script a difficult conversation with {{audience}} about: {{topic}}

Use nonviolent-communication structure: (1) observation (facts, no judgment), (2) impact, (3) the underlying need, (4) a specific, doable request. Anticipate 2 likely defensive reactions and give a calm response for each, plus opening and closing lines. Preserve the relationship and dignity throughout.

title: IEP / 504 meeting prep
desc: Strengths-based prep and family-friendly framing.
tpl:
You are a special-education teacher preparing for an IEP/504 meeting about {{name}}. Context: {{concerns}}

Provide: a strengths-first opening, the data/evidence to bring, 3 proposed accommodations with rationale, family-friendly explanations of any jargon, and 3 questions to invite the family and student voice. Keep it collaborative and hopeful.

title: Translate school jargon to plain language
desc: Make any school message clear and human.

title: Syllabus / classroom expectations
desc: Clear, positive, student- and family-friendly.
tpl:
You are a teacher writing a clear, positive syllabus for {{grade}} {{subject}}. Info to include: {{policies}}

Sections: Course overview & what we'll explore; What success looks like; Expectations (framed positively); Grading; Materials; How we communicate. Student- and family-friendly, encouraging tone, skimmable formatting. Avoid a punitive "rules" feel.

title: Review game / activity
desc: Accountable, standards-based review that's actually fun.
tpl:
You are an engagement expert. Design a {{format}} review game for {{grade}} {{subject}} on "{{topic}}".

Provide 12–15 questions sorted by difficulty (with answers), clear rules and setup, and a structure where EVERY student stays accountable (no one hiding behind a teammate). Add a quick low-tech version and a timing plan for one class period.

title: Bell ringers / warm-ups (week set)
desc: Five spiral warm-ups with answer keys.
tpl: You are a teacher who runs tight routines. Create 5 daily bell-ringers (≤5 min each) for a week of {{grade}} {{subject}} on "{{topic}}". Each should spiral a previously-taught skill AND preview today, be self-explanatory (students start without you), and include an answer key. Add one line on the routine to make warm-ups run smoothly.

title: Think-Pair-Share protocol
desc: Structured talk with frames and accountable share-out.

fields.ph: e.g. Should the character have lied?

tpl:
You are a discourse expert. Design a Think-Pair-Share for {{grade}} around: {{question}}

Give the exact timing for each phase, a "think" prompt that requires writing first, sentence frames for the "pair" talk, and an accountable share-out structure (so it's not the same 3 kids). Add one move to raise the rigor of student responses.

title: Socratic seminar plan
desc: Text-based inquiry with norms, roles and assessment.

fields.ph: e.g. a short story or ethical question

tpl:
You are a facilitation expert. Plan a Socratic seminar for {{grade}} on "{{text}}".

Provide: an opening question, 4–5 core questions (text-dependent, open-ended), 2 closing/transfer questions, seminar norms, student roles (inner/outer circle), sentence stems for respectful disagreement, and a simple participation rubric.

title: Brain breaks / energizers
desc: Quick resets matched to the mood you need.
tpl: You are a classroom-management expert. Give 5 brain breaks for {{grade}} that {{goal}} in {{time}}. For each: a name, clear step-by-step instructions, any signal to start/stop, and a smooth transition line back to work. Keep them low-prep and age-appropriate.

title: Gamify a unit or class system
desc: Light points/quests tied to real learning goals.
tpl:
You are a motivation designer. Design a light gamification system for {{grade}} {{subject}} supporting: {{goal}}.

Include: a simple points/badge/quest structure tied to LEARNING (not compliance), how students track progress, a team vs individual option, and a low-cost reward idea. Add a caution paragraph on protecting intrinsic motivation and avoiding inequity.

title: Individual behavior support plan
desc: Function-based, positive, non-punitive.

fields.ph: Describe what you see, when, how often

tpl:
You are a behavior specialist (PBIS/FBA-informed). Design a positive behavior support plan for a {{grade}} student. Behavior: {{behavior}} — likely function: {{function}}.

Include: antecedent strategies (prevent), a taught replacement behavior that meets the same need, reinforcement plan, a de-escalation step, and a simple data-tracking method. Strengths-based and non-punitive. If the function is unclear, tell me what data to collect first.

title: Restorative conversation script
desc: Repair harm, not just punish.
tpl:
You are trained in restorative practices. Script a restorative conversation for a {{grade}} situation: {{incident}}

Use restorative questions (What happened? What were you thinking/feeling? Who was affected? How can we make it right?). Keep it calm and dignity-preserving, focus on repair and future behavior, and end with a concrete agreement and follow-up. Include a note on when this is NOT appropriate.

title: Co-create class norms
desc: Student-built, positively framed agreements.
tpl:
You are a classroom-community builder. Design a 25-minute lesson for {{grade}} students to CO-CREATE class norms around: {{values}}.

Include the facilitation steps, a brainstorming structure, how to turn student ideas into 4–5 positively-framed norms (what TO do), and a commitment activity (e.g., signing/handprints). End with how to reference and reset norms later in the year.

title: Morning meeting / SEL circle
desc: Greeting, share, activity, message.
tpl: You are an SEL specialist. Plan a 15–20 min morning meeting for {{grade}} on the theme "{{theme}}" using the four components: Greeting, Sharing, Group Activity, Morning Message. Give specifics for each, 2 discussion prompts, and a closing intention. Warm, inclusive, and age-appropriate; align to a CASEL competency.

title: Transition & routine design
desc: Fast, calm routines you can teach and practice.

fields.ph: e.g. entering class, cleanup, lining up

tpl:
You are a classroom-management expert. Design an efficient routine for this {{grade}} transition: {{transition}}.

Give the exact steps, an attention signal, a target time, what students do/say, and a 3-step plan to TEACH and practice it (model, practice, reinforce). Add a reset move for when it gets sloppy.

title: In-the-moment de-escalation
desc: Calm, dignity-first steps and scripts.
tpl:
You are a crisis-prevention-trained educator. Give a calm, step-by-step de-escalation plan for this {{grade}} situation: {{situation}}.

Include: what to do with your body/voice, exact calming phrases to say (and what NOT to say), how to give the student a face-saving off-ramp, and the follow-up once calm. Protect the student's dignity and the rest of the class's safety. Note when to call for help.

title: Seating chart logic
desc: Two layouts with rationale from your notes.

fields.ph: e.g. 30 students, 2 who distract each other, 3 need front, group work often

tpl: You are a classroom-design expert. From these notes about a {{grade}} class — {{notes}} — propose 2 seating arrangements (e.g., pods vs rows/pairs) with a clear rationale for each, the trade-offs, specific pairings to make or avoid, and how the layout supports your most common activity. Describe layouts in text (a simple map is fine).

title: SEL mini-lesson
desc: 20-minute CASEL-aligned skill lesson.
tpl: You are an SEL curriculum designer. Create a 20-minute mini-lesson for {{grade}} on "{{skill}}", aligned to a CASEL competency. Structure: hook, explicit teach (define + model), guided practice/role-play, and a reflection/transfer step. Include the exact prompts and one way to reinforce the skill during the week.

title: Spiral / interleaved review set
desc: Mix skills to fight forgetting.
tpl:
You are a learning-science-informed teacher. Build a spiral review set for {{grade}} {{subject}} interleaving these skills: {{skills}}.

Mix the skills (don't block them) across 10–12 items rising in difficulty, include an answer key, and add a 2-sentence note to students on WHY mixed practice feels harder but works better (desirable difficulty).

title: Small-group intervention plan
desc: Targeted 3-session plan with progress monitoring.
tpl:
You are an interventionist. Design a 3-session small-group intervention for {{grade}} {{subject}} targeting: {{gap}}.

For each 20-minute session: objective, explicit teaching move, guided practice, and a quick check. Include a pre/post progress-monitoring measure, exit criteria (how you know they're ready to exit), and one engagement tip for reluctant students.

title: Prerequisite-skill diagnostic
desc: Check readiness before a new topic.
tpl: You are a diagnostic teacher. List the prerequisite skills students need BEFORE "{{topic}}" in {{grade}} {{subject}}. Then build a short (6–8 item) readiness diagnostic covering them, with an answer key and an interpretation guide: for each likely miss, name the gap and the quick pre-teach move.

title: Faded worked-example set
desc: Model → partial → independent with self-explanation.
tpl: You are a cognitive-load expert. Create a faded worked-example sequence for {{grade}} {{subject}} on "{{skill}}": (1) a fully worked example with reasoning annotated, (2) a partially completed one with blanks at the key decision points, (3) an independent problem. Add self-explanation prompts ("Why this step?") and an answer key.

title: Simplify multi-step directions
desc: Clear, numbered, low-language steps.
tpl:
You are an accessibility expert. Rewrite these directions for {{grade}} as clear, numbered, one-action-per-step instructions with minimal language load: {{directions}}

Use simple words and consistent verbs, suggest a visual/icon cue per step where helpful, bold the key action word in each step, and add a one-line "you're done when…" success check.

title: Plain, translation-ready family message
desc: Simple English + Spanish version.
tpl:
You are a multilingual family-engagement specialist. Rewrite this message in simple, translation-ready English (short sentences, no idioms or slang): {{message}}

Then provide a natural Spanish translation. Keep the tone warm and the meaning exact. Flag anything culturally sensitive to double-check with a bilingual colleague.

title: Graphic organizer designer
desc: Pick and lay out the right organizer for a task.

fields.ph: e.g. compare 2 things, sequence events, cause/effect

tpl: You are an instructional designer. Recommend the BEST graphic organizer for this {{grade}} thinking task: {{task}}. Explain why it fits, then lay it out in text (boxes, columns, arrows described clearly) with guiding prompts in each section and a completed mini-example so students see the target.

title: Make a resource accessible
desc: Concrete UDL/accessibility upgrades.

title: Weekly plan from standards
desc: Turn standards into a day-by-day plan table.
tpl:
You are an efficient planner. Turn this week's {{grade}} {{subject}} standards into a day-by-day plan: {{standards}}

Output a TABLE: Day | objective | activity/mini-lesson | formative check | homework. Balance pacing and cognitive load, build on the prior day, and end the week with a check for understanding. Keep activities realistic for one class period.

title: PLC / team meeting agenda
desc: Focused, time-boxed, decisions-oriented.
tpl:
You are a PLC facilitator. Build a {{minutes}} agenda focused on: {{topic}}.

Include time-boxed items, a clear objective and desired outcome, protocols for any data/discussion, assigned roles (facilitator/timekeeper/notetaker), and a "decisions & next steps (who/what/when)" closing section. Keep it action-oriented, not just talk.

title: Classroom grant / DonorsChoose pitch
desc: Compelling, specific funding request.

fields.ph: Describe your students and the need

tpl:
You are a persuasive grant writer. Write a classroom funding pitch for {{grade}} requesting: {{resource}}. Context: {{impact}}

Structure: a vivid, specific opening about your students; the concrete need; exactly how this resource changes learning; and a warm thank-you. Honest and heartfelt (no exaggeration), concrete details over adjectives, ~180 words. Add a short project title.

title: Professional email (admin/colleague)
desc: Clear, respectful, with a specific ask.

fields.ph: What you need and any context

tpl:
You are a professional communicator. Draft an email that accomplishes: {{purpose}}. Tone: {{tone}}.

Keep it concise and scannable, lead with the ask or key point, give only the necessary context, and end with a clear next step/deadline. Provide a specific subject line. Avoid over-apologizing or burying the request.

title: Self-evaluation / reflection
desc: Framework-aligned, evidence-based statements.

fields.ph: Bullet what you did and its impact

tpl:
You are an instructional coach helping a teacher write a self-evaluation{{framework}}. From this evidence: {{evidence}}

Draft reflective statements that pair specific evidence with impact on students, name one genuine growth area with a concrete goal, and use professional, non-defensive language. Keep it honest and grounded, not boastful.

title: Substitute folder checklist
desc: Everything a guest teacher needs, organized.
tpl:
You are an organized teacher. Create a complete substitute-folder checklist for {{grade}} {{subject}}, plus a fill-in "About My Class" one-pager template.

Cover: daily schedule, seating/roster, routines & signals, behavior management, key students (helpers, medical, allergies) framed appropriately, emergency procedures, tech logins, and where to leave notes for me. Make the one-pager a clean template with [blanks] to fill.

title: Math problem set (scaffolded + solutions)
desc: Standards-based problems, easy→hard, with worked solutions.
tpl:
You are a math curriculum specialist. Create {{count}} problems for {{grade}} on "{{skill}}", scaffolded from straightforward to challenging{{context}}.

Include at least 2 multi-step/reasoning problems. Provide FULL worked solutions (show the steps and reasoning), and for any tempting wrong path, name the misconception it comes from. Use inclusive names/contexts. Label each problem's difficulty.

title: Real-world math word problems
desc: Engaging, multi-step problems on a theme, with a reasoning rubric.
tpl:
You are a math teacher who makes math feel real. Write 6 engaging word problems for {{grade}} on "{{skill}}" set in the context of {{theme}}. Vary structure so students can't pattern-match; include 2 multi-step problems and 1 with extra (distractor) information.

Provide answers with reasoning, and a short 3-level rubric for evaluating student REASONING (not just the final number). Use culturally inclusive names and situations.

title: Math misconception diagnostic
desc: Top misconceptions, a probe for each, and reteach moves.
tpl: You are a math education researcher. For "{{concept}}" in {{grade}}, list the 4–5 most common student misconceptions. For EACH: explain why it makes intuitive sense to students, give one diagnostic item that would reveal it, and a targeted reteach move (with a better representation or model). End with the single highest-impact misconception to tackle first.

title: Number talk / math routine
desc: A problem string with anticipated strategies and questions.
tpl:
You are a number-talks expert. Design a 10-minute number talk for {{grade}} focused on "{{focus}}".

Give a purposeful problem STRING (3–4 problems sequenced to surface and connect strategies), the strategies you anticipate students will use for each, the teacher questions that advance mathematical discourse, and how to record/connect student thinking visually. Keep it mental-math (no algorithms rushed in).

title: 3-Act math task
desc: Perplexing hook, info on request, reveal + extension.
tpl:
You are a math task designer (Dan Meyer style). Design a 3-Act task for {{grade}} on "{{concept}}".

Act 1: a perplexing real situation and the one compelling question (kept low-floor); what students notice/wonder. Act 2: the information students will request and how they'd use it. Act 3: the reveal and a sequel/extension question. Include facilitation notes and the underlying math. Make Act 1 need no numbers.

title: Science CER scaffold
desc: Claim–Evidence–Reasoning with frames and rubric.

fields.ph: e.g. why the ice melted faster on metal

tpl:
You are an NGSS science teacher. Build a Claim–Evidence–Reasoning scaffold for {{grade}} on this phenomenon: {{phenomenon}}.

Provide: a guiding question, sentence frames for Claim, Evidence, and Reasoning separately, a graphic-organizer layout, a student-friendly CER rubric, and one exemplar STRONG response plus one weak response with a note on why. Emphasize connecting evidence to a science principle in the reasoning.

title: Science lab / investigation
desc: Testable question, variables, procedure, safety, analysis.

fields.ph: e.g. what affects how fast a reaction happens
e.g. only household materials, 1 class period

tpl:
You are a science teacher and safety officer. Design a hands-on investigation for {{grade}} on: {{question}}. Constraints: {{constraints}}.

Include: a testable question, a hypothesis frame, clearly labeled variables (independent, dependent, controlled), a step-by-step procedure, a data table, explicit SAFETY notes, and analysis questions that push toward a conclusion (including sources of error). Note one extension for early finishers.

title: Phenomenon-based NGSS lesson
desc: 3-dimensional lesson (DCI + SEP + CCC).

fields.ph: e.g. a can crushed by cooling

tpl:
You are an NGSS curriculum designer. Design a phenomenon-based lesson for {{grade}} anchored in: {{phenomenon}}{{dci}}.

Make it 3-dimensional: name the Disciplinary Core Idea, one Science & Engineering Practice students DO, and one Crosscutting Concept. Provide a driving question, a notice/wonder opener, the investigation or modeling activity, a formative check, and how students revise their model. Keep students explaining the phenomenon, not just reading about it.

title: Engineering design challenge
desc: Full EDP challenge with criteria, constraints, rubric.

fields.ph: e.g. build a bridge that holds weight

tpl:
You are a STEM/engineering teacher. Design an Engineering Design Process challenge for {{grade}}: {{challenge}}. Materials: {{materials}}.

Structure it through Ask → Imagine → Plan → Create → Test → Improve. Give clear success CRITERIA and CONSTRAINTS, a testing/measurement method, roles for teamwork, a reflection on iteration (what they'd change), and an analytic rubric. Connect it to a real math/science concept.

title: CS / coding activity
desc: Teach a concept unplugged, Scratch or Python.
tpl:
You are a computer-science teacher. Design an activity teaching "{{concept}}" to {{grade}} in this mode: {{mode}}.

Include: a relatable analogy for the concept, a warm-up, a guided task with clear steps, a challenge/extension, and the common bugs or misconceptions to watch for (with a fix for each). Keep the cognitive load appropriate and the entry point low. Add a quick check for understanding.

title: Data analysis / graphing task
desc: Realistic dataset, rising-DOK questions, 'what it doesn't say'.

fields.ph: e.g. rainfall by month, class survey

tpl:
You are a math/data teacher. Create a data task for {{grade}} on "{{skill}}" using a small, realistic dataset about {{context}} (invent believable numbers and present them in a table).

Ask questions rising in Depth of Knowledge: read the data → interpret/compute → infer/justify. Include an answer key, and finish with a discussion prompt on what the data does NOT tell us (limitations, correlation vs causation as appropriate).

title: Math discourse questions
desc: Assessing/advancing questions to promote reasoning.

fields.ph: Paste the math problem students are working

tpl:
You are a math-discourse expert (5 Practices). For this {{grade}} problem — {{problem}} — generate teacher questions that promote reasoning over answer-getting:

• 3 ASSESSING questions (make student thinking visible)
• 3 ADVANCING questions (push toward the math goal without telling)
• 2 "convince me / justify" prompts
Plus 2 sentence frames for students to explain and critique reasoning. Note the likely strategies students will use so I can sequence the share-out.

title: STEM project + rubric
desc: Integrated, driving-question project with milestones.
tpl:
You are a STEM curriculum designer. Design an integrated STEM project for {{grade}} on "{{topic}}" that connects science, math, and engineering.

Include: a driving question, the specific science and math concepts applied, an engineering/build component, a milestone timeline, teamwork roles, a real-world deliverable/audience, and an analytic rubric assessing content AND process (collaboration, iteration). Keep it rigorous and doable with common materials.
